title: Vajranabha Demands the Three Worlds
story:
On the summit of Mount Sumeru, an Asura sat in austerities so severe that the grandfather of the worlds himself took notice. Vajranabha was no ordinary demon, and he wanted no ordinary power: he wanted to be unkillable, and he wanted a home that nothing could enter. When Brahma, pleased by his penance, appeared before him and offered a boon, the Asura asked for two gifts — that even the gods might never be able to kill him, and that he might possess the city Vajra, where even the air could not enter without his will, a city that gave its lord whatever he desired before he had even thought of it, ringed by gardens and walls, surrounded by branch cities, full of peerless gems.

Brahma granted both, and Vajranabha moved into Vajra. Millions of demons came to live there under his protection, filling the central city, its gardens and its many charming branch cities, healthy and well-fed and contented, while their king enjoyed the boon he had demanded. No enemy had ever been known to pass those walls, and no one in the three worlds had found the door.

For a time that satisfied him. Then pride finished what penance had begun: the king of the Asuras decided the three worlds were not the gods' to keep. He stood before Indra, the king of heaven, and announced: "All the three worlds are the common property of the high-souled sons of Kashyapa. I wish to govern the three worlds. If you do not approve of my proposal, give me battle."

Indra answered with patience instead of war. He consulted Brihaspati, the priest of the gods, and then said: "Our father, the ascetic Kashyapa, is now engaged in a sacrifice. When it is finished, he will do what is fair." Vajranabha carried the same demand to Kashyapa himself, and heard the same words: go back to Vajra, live self-controlled, and wait for the sacrifice to end.

The demon returned to his city to wait — and while he waited, the gods were not idle. Indra went secretly to Dwaraka and told Krishna everything Vajranabha had said. Krishna's answer was calm and complete: "My father's horse-sacrifice is at hand. When it is over, I will kill Vajranabha. But even the wind cannot enter his city unless he wishes it, so we will find our own way in."

The way in was already taking shape. During the horse-sacrifice, a wandering actor named Bhadra so charmed the assembled sages with his art that they offered him any boon he desired. Prompted — the text says it plainly — by Krishna's wish and the goddess of learning herself, Bhadra asked for strange gifts: to range freely over the earth and the sky, to be slain by no creature mobile or immobile, to take any form he pleased, to be never touched by age, and to find the sages always pleased with him. The Munis said "So be it," and Bhadra became the one being in all creation who could go anywhere and be welcomed everywhere. He began to wander the cities of the demon kings, performing for the Danavas, and on every festival day he came to Dwaraka, where the Yadavas received him as a guest of honour.

The plan was quiet, and it was already complete. And in heaven, Indra was speaking to the swans — the celestial birds who, though they carried the gods and the pious across the sky, were his own brothers, begotten by Kashyapa. To them he spoke of the great duty that now lay before the gods: the destruction of their enemies.
reflection: The boon that made Vajranabha untouchable also made him predictable: a king who cannot be killed and a city that cannot be entered will be defeated through exactly that logic — by someone who can go anywhere and take any form. Boons answer words, not intentions, and pride read his own wish as a promise of safety.
next_story_tease: The actor's boon was the key to Vajra — and soon the Yadavas would carry it through the city's unbreachable gates disguised as a company of players.
hero_scene: Vajranabha kneeling in austerity on the snow of Mount Sumeru as Brahma appears before him, while behind him a vision of the walled city Vajra with its gardens and branch cities rises in the sky.
